Introduction - June 2011 











##### **Prices come under renewed pressure** 

In our previous monthly reports we have focused on our underlying view that, given the current elevated base metal prices, a constant stream of bullish news is required to support these levels.  Our conclusion was that “we do not believe that this ‘news flow’ will be maintained and we are cautious about the prospects for further price increases”. Obviously this bullish news flow did dry up and the GFMS Base Metal Index fell from a recent peak of 401.47 in Apr

il to 344.42 in early June. 

The performance of the individual metals in the recent correction largely reflected earlier price moves rather than the specific underlying fundamentals.  Aluminium prices have held up better than those across the rest of the sector, while the recent peak-to-trough fall for tin was the largest. This reflects the previous surge in tin prices rather than aluminium having the superior underlying fundamentals. 

The trigger for the correction partly reflects concerns about the rate of economic growth going forward.  Also there is the recognition that the inventory rebuild that helped to support the exceptionally strong demand growth in 2010 will not be such an issue in 2011.  One feature of the market has been the general decline in imports of base metals by China – this has been a particular feature of the copper market. 

While economic growth rates within the country will remain high, the fear is that attempts to rein in inflation and curb the property bubble will lead to a slowdown in the rate of expansion.  Another trigger behind the recent decline in base metal prices has been the strengthening of the dollar, which might better be described as a weakening of the euro.  The return of the issue of sovereign debt (not that it ever really went away) added to the mix.  There are also concerns about what the post Quantitative Easing Two (QE2) environment will look like.  If there is not a QE3 then interest rates will 

rise, which would put further pressure on the commodity complex.  Apart from funds switching their asset allocation to reflect this move, a higher interest rate environment could see some of the long-term warehousing deals unravel. 

###### **Demand environment is unchanged for now** 

Given the exceptionally high prices both from a historical context, and in relation to the marginal costs of production, markets are always vulnerable to a correction.  However, at this stage most of the demand indicators remain positive.  In the economics section, we look at some of the forward-looking economic indicators, which in most cases are pointing to continued growth.  Although data on nonferrous semis shipments and downstream steel shipments are lagging rather than leading indicators, apart from the earthquake related dip in Japan, most of these statistics suggest that demand is holding up well.  This view is reinforced by the anecdotal evidence that we receive and by the increases in physical premiums.  We believe that a reasonably strong demand backdrop will help limit the downside.  On previous corrections it was by no means just the funds that saw a buying opportunity.  We have also noted increased buying by consumers on any significant dips. 

###### **Supply side may eventually kick back in** 

We note above that the key to recent price movements for the individual metals has been the earlier price performance with those that had lagged the market earlier in the cycle holding up the best.  There is, in our vi

ew, only so long that such a trend can remain in place. We believe that supply factors will once again influence relative price changes. Nothing has changed over the last month to alter our view on the supply. In our view, the index is likely to remain on a downward trend in the coming months as a result of the above-mentioned factors. Trends in the ISM manufacturing index as well as in the construction and automotive sectors in the United States The auto sector displayed a similar trend, with vehicle sales falling by almost 10% to 11.8 million units on a seasonally adjusted annualised rate in May, notably interrupting a steady upward march. Diminished inventories of Japanese vehicles were only partly to blame. High fuel prices and fewer sales incentives arguably caused more potential buyers to sit on the sidelines. Housing starts also came in weak in April, falling to an annualised rate of 523,000 units, a notable 10.6% down on March’s level of 585,000 units. Bad weather in the South and concerns over rising oil prices likely weighed on construction. Falling permit issuance indicates that housing starts are unlikely to pick up by much over the next few months. ###### **Market background** Although not immune from the correction in industrial commodities, aluminium has once again outperformed the rest of the base metal sector. The average cash quote in May fell by just 2.6% to $2,592/tonne compared to a decline in the GFMS Base Metal Index of 9.2% last month. The GFMS BMI gives equal weight to the individual base metals. Aluminium prices have also rallied in late May and in early June and now are in excess of $2,600/tonne. As we have noted in our previou

s reports, the relatively strong performance has come about with little fundamental support. 

As ever there is issue of the massive LME stockpile; that is overhanging the market. We believe that the environment of higher interest rates that is emerging will lead to some of this metal being released back into the market.  From a broader perspective, the massive LME stockpile is unlikely to be drawn down given the underlying fundamentals which implies that the recent out-performance of the aluminium may begin to lose some momentum. 

Cumulative production in the first four months of the year was 6.9% up on the corresponding period of 2010.  We expect the recent uptrend in Chinese output to continue. Figures from Chinese Non-Ferrous Industry Association show daily output at 48,382 tonnes in April up from 45,643 tonnes in March set a new record high of 1.46m tonnes in April, 6.9% up on a year earlier. 

###### **Stock levels remain high despite the price advance** 

LME inventories have been fairly stable and are around 4.7 million tonnes in early June, over 300,000 tonnes higher than at the start of the year.  Stocks of unwrought aluminium held by producers as reported by the International Aluminium Association (IAI) have also trended higher, rising by just over 115,000 tonnes in the first four months of this year to 1.514 million tonnes.  The increase has largely been down to North America.  The region saw inventories climb by 149,000 tonnes to 376,000 tonnes.  This reflects the sharp increase to production (see below for details), which appears to have outstripped demand. The other main source of visible inventory are the SHFE stocks, which show a near 70,000 tonne reduction so far this year and in early May stood at around 375,000 tonnes. 

###### **Chinese government tries to rein in capacity** 

In our earlier research we have detailed the plans of the Chinese government to curb overcapacity via The National Development and Reform Commission (NDRC).  However as detailed before this has had no impact on production levels, which in late 2010 was cut back.  There are a number of issues driving the Chinese supply side. First are the attempts by the government to reduce in-efficient capacity.  The government has issued a circular to “curb overcapacity of aluminium smelting and prevent redundant construction of aluminium smelter projects”.  There are currently 23 proposed projects with a combined capacity of 7.74 million tonnes per year (tpy). This, in theory, could take Chinese capacity to 30 million tpy by 2015.  Last year, output was 17.6 million tonnes and capacity was 22.5 million tpy. The problem remains that attempts curb output are being more than offset by additions to capacity. We note that the construction of an 800,000 tpy smelter has recently commenced in the Xinjiang province. ###### **Growth beginning to slow outside of China** Although production outside of China is still showing yearon-year gains in excess of 5%, output has levelled out over the last three months. Between January and April, daily production was fairly stable at around 69,500 tpd with main growth in the Gulf and North America. It is forecast that output in the former region will exceed 4 million tonnes this year given the commissioning and ramp up of the Qatalum and Emal smelters. Norsk Hydro’s Qatalum smelter in Qatar, which came on stream in late 2009, is expected to produce around 500,000 tonnes of primary aluminium this year. ###### **Mixed fortunes in the Americas** The impact of the restart of US smelters is clearly shown in the latest Aluminum Association data. US primary output in the first four months of the year was 9.6% higher at 614,605 tonnes, while output in April was 13.6% up yearon year. This uptrend is set to continue. As we noted in the previous issue of the Base Metals One Year Forecast, Ormet Corporation, has recently restored its aluminium smelter to full capacity that should boost output by 82,000 tonnes this year. Ormet’s total production capacity with six potlines is about 266,000 tpy. Century Aluminium has also ramped up production at its Hannibal smelter, while Alcoa is bringing online idled lines at its Massena East, Wenatchee and Intalco smelters. One area of lower production continues to be Brazil. According to ABAL, the industry organisation, output in April was down 6.2% year-on-year at 118,400 tonnes. Output at Votorantim registered a 15.2% decline to 32,900 tonnes due to planned maintenance work. Production at Novelis fell by nearly 50% to 4,100 tonnes, reflecting the permanent closure of its 60,000 tpy Aratu smelter in December last year due to high power and operating costs. Modest increases were recorded at Alcoa and BHP Billiton’s operations in the country. ###### **Conflicting signals from the demand side** As highlighted in the Executive Summa

ry and the Economics section, there are a number of concerns about the sustainability of robust economic growth that has supported aluminium consumption. At this stage, this has yet to have significant impact on the market. However in our view we could see easier demand conditions in the second half of the year. At the moment, premiums are holding firm at high levels. In Singapore, premiums are in a range of $85-90/ tonne, while in Indonesia and Thailand they are reported to be as high as $120/tonne. Reflecting steady demand in Europe, premiums for duty-paid physical aluminium have improved, with Rotterdam material in the range of $190-210/tonne, up from $185-200/tonne at the end of the first quarter. Meanwhile, premiums for duty-unpaid material are at $130-135/tonne, close to their highest levels since June last year. In North America, it appears that strong demand growth and higher transport costs are supporting higher physical premiums. The latter has played a particularly important role with a severe shortage of trucks; a situation that has been exacerbated by the flooding of the Ohio River which has seen companies use trucks rather than river barges. US Midwest spot premiums rose from $143-154/tonne in March to a range of $200-220/tonne in early June. ###### **Short-term (and underlying) weakness in Japanese demand...** In Japan, we have the situation whereby although physical premiums appear to be holding up, other indicators confirm the weakness in the market. Premiums for the third quarter have been set at around $120/tonne up from $113/tonne in the second quarter. Aluminium semis shipments are less encouraging. GFMS’ outlook for the tin market is largely unchanged from our previous report.  Although a considerable correction has been seen over the past month, we still expect that tin’s strong market fundamentals will provide essential support to prices over both the short and longer term. and the ongoing problems in major producing countries. On the demand side, whilst in part reflective of a slowdown in end-use demand from the high base, we note that a significant proportion of the recent weakness in Chinese apparent consumption has come from the destocking of materials accumulated earlier within the country. In our view, given our expectations for robust end-use growth in the country this year, any further price weakness from current levels is expected to result in a reversal of this trend, providing a floor to prices. Indeed, we expect China to continue to be the key driver of demand growth going forward, especially given the expected slowdown in growth in the mature economies. Regarding our price forecasts, we expect tin prices to recover some lost ground in the coming months as the market tightens. Indeed, in looking at the latest stock changes at the LME, a slight reversal of the uptrend in inventory levels from the end of May could be an early sign of buyers returning to the market. Thus, we expect prices to average $29,700/tonne over the second quarter. A recovery in demand and ongoing supply-side constraints will continue to drive gains over the second half of 2011 and over the first quarter of 2012, by which time we expect prices to average $35,000/tonne.
